title: SCHUFA Holding (Scoring), 7 December 2023
text: Operative part: Article 22(1) GDPR 'must be interpreted as meaning that the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning his or her ability to meet payment commitments in the future constitutes "automated individual decision-making" within the meaning of that provision, where a third party, to which that probability value is transmitted, draws strongly on that probability value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.' Para. 52: Article 22(1) 'lays down a prohibition in principle'. Consequence for claims: a recommendation must remain advice that a claims handler weighs and can depart from; if handlers in practice draw strongly on it, the recommendation itself risks being the decision.

title: EDPS v SRB, 4 September 2025
text: Judgment on Regulation 2018/1725 (EU institutions), whose definitions match the GDPR. Operative part: sets aside the General Court's judgment in T-557/20 and refers the case back. Para. 86: pseudonymised data 'must not be regarded as constituting, in all cases and for every person, personal data', in so far as pseudonymisation may 'effectively prevent persons other than the controller from identifying the data subject'. Para. 77: that presupposes that the recipient cannot lift the measures and that the measures prevent attribution 'including by recourse to other means of identification such as cross-checking with other factors'. Paras. 111 and 112: for the duty to inform about recipients, identifiability is assessed 'at the time of collection of the data and from the point of view of the controller', irrespective of whether the data are personal for the recipient. Consequence: placeholders lower the risk of a cloud transfer, but the insurer still treats the data as personal, names the recipients in its privacy notice and records the transfer.

title: OT v Vyriausioji tarnybinės etikos komisija, 1 August 2022
text: Operative part, point 2: Article 9(1) GDPR covers the publication of 'personal data that are liable to disclose indirectly the sexual orientation of a natural person'. Para. 127: the special-category regime is not excluded for 'personal data that are liable indirectly to reveal sensitive information'. Para. 120 frames the test as data revealing a special category 'by means of an intellectual operation involving comparison or deduction'. Consequence: an invoice line, medication or hospital name from which a health condition can be deduced is health data.

title: Test-Achats, 1 March 2011
text: Operative part: 'Article 5(2) of Council Directive 2004/113/EC ... is invalid with effect from 21 December 2012.' That provision let Member States keep sex-based differences in insurance premiums and benefits; para. 32 finds it 'incompatible with Articles 21 and 23 of the Charter'. The case is about sex, not ethnicity; for ethnic origin the controlling rule is Directive 2000/43/EC, Art. 2 and Art. 3(1)(h) (access to goods and services). Consequence: insurance premiums and benefits may not differ by sex, and selecting claims by ethnic origin or a proxy for it is discrimination.

title: Breyer, 19 October 2016
text: Operative part, point 1: a dynamic IP address is personal data for a website operator 'where the latter has the legal means which enable it to identify the data subject with additional data which the internet service provider has about that person'. Para. 46: a means is not reasonably likely to be used where identification is 'prohibited by law or practically impossible', so that 'the risk of identification appears in reality to be insignificant'. Consequence: identifiability counts the means a party can lawfully obtain through someone else, so a recipient that can link a placeholder back through another party still holds personal data.

title: EDPB Guidelines 01/2025 on pseudonymisation (adopted 16 January 2025, version for public consultation)
text: Executive summary: 'Pseudonymised data, which could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information, is to be considered information on an identifiable natural person, and is therefore personal. This statement also holds true if pseudonymised data and additional information are not in the hands of the same person.' Pseudonymisation may 'help guarantee an essentially equivalent level of protection for data they intend to export', but 'pseudonymisation alone will normally not be a sufficient measure'. The controller defines a pseudonymisation domain and keeps the additional information (the key) outside it.

title: Guidelines on automated decision-making and profiling (WP251rev.01)
text: Page 21: 'The controller cannot avoid the Article 22 provisions by fabricating human involvement.' Human oversight must be 'meaningful, rather than just a token gesture. It should be carried out by someone who has the authority and competence to change the decision. As part of the analysis, they should consider all the relevant data.' Page 23: a controller relying on the contract exception in Art. 22(2)(a) 'must be able to show that this type of processing is necessary, taking into account whether a less privacy-intrusive method could be adopted.'

title: EIOPA Opinion on AI governance and risk management, EIOPA-BoS-25-360, 6 August 2025
text: Para. 2.4: the AI Act identifies as high-risk 'the use of AI systems for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance'. Paras. 2.5 and 2.6: the Opinion covers insurance AI systems that are not prohibited or high-risk; para. 2.1 names claims management as one such use. Para. 3.7: undertakings should develop risk-based and proportionate governance covering fairness and ethics, data governance, documentation and record keeping, transparency and explainability, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. Para. 3.28: customers should be informed that they are interacting with an AI system and, on request, told the influence of the AI system on a decision with a material impact on them.

title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: LLM01 Prompt Injection
text: Summary: instructions embedded in user input or documents can alter an LLM's behaviour. Mitigations include constraining model behaviour, segregating untrusted content, requiring human approval for privileged actions, and enforcing decisions outside the model.
